La luz del Sol es una mezcla de ondas el: Sunlight is a mixture of electromagnetic waves of many wavelengths at once. The eye sees those between about 400 nm (violet) and about 700 nm (red); together they look white.\n\nThey all travel at the same speed in vacuum, $c = λ f = 3·10^8 "m/s"$, but each colour has its own $λ$: the blue wave measures about 450 nm and the red one, about 700 nm.

El aire es sobre todo nitrógeno y oxígen: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and its molecules measure about $0.3 "nm"$: fifteen hundred times less than the wavelength of blue light. For the wave, each molecule is a point.\n\nThe electric field of the light pulls the nucleus to one side and the electron cloud to the other, and separates them a little: the molecule becomes a dipole $p = α E$ that oscillates at the frequency of the light, $f = c/λ = 6.7·10^14 "Hz"$ for blue.
Un dipolo que oscila emite luz hacia tod: An oscillating dipole emits light in all directions

Una carga que oscila radia una onda en t: An oscillating charge radiates a wave in all directions, except along its axis. The power emitted by a dipole is proportional to $ω^4 p^2$: it grows with the fourth power of the frequency, that is, it decreases with the fourth power of the wavelength.\n\nThis is Rayleigh scattering, $I ∝ 1/λ^4$. Blue light is not "reflected" in one place: each molecule absorbs it and re-emits it sideways, and so it reaches your eyes from any point of the sky, not only from the Sun.

Con $I ∝ 1/λ^4$, el azul (450 nm) se dis: With $I ∝ 1/λ^4$, blue (450 nm) is scattered $(700/450)^4 = 5.9$ times more than red, and violet (400 nm), $(700/400)^4 = 9.4$ times. That is why the sky is not red.\n\nThen why is it not violet? Because the Sun emits less violet light than blue, part of it is absorbed by the upper atmosphere and the eye is much less sensitive to violet. What reaches the eye is a pale blue, mixed with some green and violet.
